claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claims.claim: VAP27-1-GFP is localized to the ER in Arabidopsis leaf epidermal cells, forming some puncta.
claims.source: VAP27-1-GFP is localized to the ER in Arabidopsis leaf epidermal cells, forming some puncta (although fewer than reported for VAP27-1 when transiently overexpressed in tobacco; Wang et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from confocal microscopy and citations to previous studies (Wang et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2016).

claims.claim: The VAP27-1 localization pattern was similar in msl10-1, msl10-3G, and their segregated WT MSL10 backgrounds.
claims.source: We found that the VAP27-1 localization pattern was similar in msl10-1, msl10-3G, and their segregated WT MSL10 backgrounds (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Due to the presumed synthetic lethality, the effect of MSL10 on VAP27-3 EPCSs could not be assessed.
claims.source: Due to the presumed synthetic lethality described above, we were unable to assess the effect of MSL10 on VAP27-3 EPCSs.
claims.evidence: The manuscript describes a limitation of the experimental approach.

claims.claim: SYT1-GFP displayed the expected punctate localization.
claims.source: SYT1-GFP displayed the expected punctate localization (Levy et al., 2015; Pérez-Sancho et al., 2015), and SYT1-GFP localization was unchanged in the msl10-1 background (Figure 4E and F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E and citations to previous studies (Levy et al., 2015; Pérez-Sancho et al., 2015).

claims.claim: SYT1-GFP localization was unchanged in the msl10-1 background.
claims.source: SYT1-GFP displayed the expected punctate localization (Levy et al., 2015; Pérez-Sancho et al., 2015), and SYT1-GFP localization was unchanged in the msl10-1 background (Figure 4E and F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claims.claim: In the msl10-3G background, SYT1-GFP puncta were expanded in leaf epidermal cells compared to the WT.
claims.source: However, in the msl10-3G background, SYT1-GFP puncta were expanded in leaf epidermal cells compared to the WT, leading to a modest, but significant increase in SYT1-GFP area relative to cellular area (Figure 4E and G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E and G.

claims.claim: The expansion of SYT1-GFP puncta in msl10-3G led to a modest, but significant increase in SYT1-GFP area relative to cellular area.
claims.source: However, in the msl10-3G background, SYT1-GFP puncta were expanded in leaf epidermal cells compared to the WT, leading to a modest, but significant increase in SYT1-GFP area relative to cellular area (Figure 4E and G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: The SYT1-GFP pattern in msl10-3G closely resembled that observed with the MAPPER-GFP marker.
claims.source: This SYT1-GFP pattern closely resembled that observed with the MAPPER-GFP marker (compare Figure 4A and D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparing data shown in Figure 4A and D.

claims.claim: SYT-EPCSs are sensitive to environmental conditions, quickly changing localization in response to mechanical pressure and slowly remodeling in response to freezing and salinity stress and the presence of rare ions.
claims.source: SYT-EPCSs are sensitive to environmental conditions, quickly changing localization in response to mechanical pressure (Pérez-Sancho et al., 2015) and slowly remodeling in response to freezing and salinity stress and the presence of rare ions (Lee et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2020; Ruiz-Lopez et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Pérez-Sancho et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2020; Ruiz-Lopez et al., 2021).

claims.claim: EPCSs marked by MAPPER-GFP in cotyledon epidermal cells expanded after a 16 hr exposure to 100 mM NaCl.
claims.source: As previously reported (Lee et al., 2019), EPCSs marked by MAPPER-GFP in cotyledon epidermal cells expanded after a 16 hr exposure to 100 mM NaCl (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and a citation to a previous study (Lee et al., 2019).

claims.claim: A similar MAPPER-GFP localization pattern was observed in msl10-1 and msl10-3G seedlings treated with NaCl.
claims.source: A similar MAPPER-GFP localization pattern was also observed in msl10-1 and msl10-3G seedlings treated with NaCl, indicating that MSL10 does not influence the expansion of EPCSs during salinity stress.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: MSL10 does not influence the expansion of EPCSs during salinity stress.
claims.source: A similar MAPPER-GFP localization pattern was also observed in msl10-1 and msl10-3G seedlings treated with NaCl, indicating that MSL10 does not influence the expansion of EPCSs during salinity stress.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that MAPPER-GFP localization was similar in WT, msl10-1, and msl10-3G seedlings treated with NaCl.

claims.claim: Salinity-induced EPCS expansion is reversible when seedlings are moved to media lacking NaCl, triggering a hypo-osmotic shock.
claims.source: Salinity-induced EPCS expansion is reversible when seedlings are moved to media lacking NaCl, triggering a hypo-osmotic shock (Lee et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Lee et al., 2019).

claims.claim: MSL10 plays a role in the cellular response to hypo-osmotic cell swelling.
claims.source: As MSL10 plays a role in the cellular response to hypo-osmotic cell swelling (Basu and Haswell, 2020a), we asked whether MSL10 was also responsible for EPCS shrinking under these conditions.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Basu and Haswell, 2020a).

claims.claim: MAPPER-GFP signal decreased in cotyledon epidermal cells 24 hr after hypo-osmotic shock.
claims.source: We found that MAPPER-GFP signal decreased in cotyledon epidermal cells 24 hr after hypo-osmotic shock (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) but that this phenomenon was unaffected by the msl10-1 or msl10-3G alleles.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The decrease in MAPPER-GFP signal after hypo-osmotic shock was unaffected by the msl10-1 or msl10-3G alleles.
claims.source: We found that MAPPER-GFP signal decreased in cotyledon epidermal cells 24 hr after hypo-osmotic shock (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) but that this phenomenon was unaffected by the msl10-1 or msl10-3G alleles.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: SYT1-GFP has been reported to move from a 'beads on a string' localization pattern to a punctate one when mechanical stress is applied.
claims.source: SYT1-GFP has been reported to move from a 'beads on a string' localization pattern to a punctate one when mechanical stress is applied (Pérez-Sancho et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Pérez-Sancho et al., 2015).

claims.claim: SYT1-GFP localization always appeared punctate in cotyledon epidermal cells, and no appreciable change in this localization was seen when pressure was added.
claims.source: In our hands, SYT1-GFP localization always appeared punctate in cotyledon epidermal cells, and we did not see an appreciable change in this localization when pressure was added (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: A forward genetic screen was performed using the obvious growth defect of msl10-3G plants as the basis of a visual screen.
claims.source: We used the obvious growth defect of msl10-3G plants (Zou et al., 2016; Basu et al., 2020b) as the basis of a visual screen, as illustrated in Figure 5A.
claims.evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental approach used.

claims.claim: EMS-induced suppressor mutants, referred to as suppressed death from msl10-3G (sdm), were initially isolated based on increased height compared to parental msl10-3G plants in the M1 and M2 generations.
claims.source: EMS-induced suppressor mutants, referred to as suppressed death from msl10-3G (sdm), were initially isolated based on increased height compared to parental msl10-3G plants in the M1 and M2 generations.
claims.evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental approach used.

claims.claim: MSL10 exons were sequenced in all 40 mutant lines.
claims.source: As msl10-3G plants share some of the characteristics of lesionmimic-mutants (Basu et al., 2022), and intragenic mutations are particularly common in suppressor screens of lesionmimic mutants (van Wersch et al., 2016), we sequenced MSL10 exons in all 40 mutant lines.
claims.evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental approach used.

claims.claim: 35 of the 40 mutant lines had a missense mutation in the MSL10 coding or splice-junction sequences.
claims.source: Indeed, 35 had a missense mutation in the MSL10 coding or splice-junction sequences (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The five remaining sdm mutants were presumed to have extragenic suppressor mutations.
claims.source: The five remaining sdm mutants were presumed to have extragenic suppressor mutations.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the absence of mutations in MSL10 exons.

claims.claim: The mapping-by-sequencing strategy successfully identified extragenic suppressor mutations for two of the five sdm mutants, sdm26 and sdm34.
claims.source: The mapping-by-sequencing strategy we employed (see below) successfully identified extragenic suppressor mutations for two of these , sdm26 and sdm34.
claims.evidence: The manuscript describes the results of the mapping-by-sequencing strategy.

claims.claim: sdm26 and sdm34 mutant plants were taller than msl10-3G plants but not as tall as WT plants.
claims.source: Notably, sdm26 and sdm34 mutant plants were taller than msl10-3G plants but not as tall as WT plants (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The offspring of both sdm26 and sdm34 backcrosses to msl10-3G (BC1F1 plants) were as tall as their sdm parents.
claims.source: The offspring of both sdm26 and sdm34 backcrosses to msl10-3G (BC1F1 plants) were as tall as their sdm parents (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: In the BC1F2 generation, plants with intermediate height (sdm phenotype) were present approximately 3:1 relative to those with the msl10-3G dwarf phenotype.
claims.source: Furthermore, in the BC1F2 generation, plants with intermediate height (sdm phenotype) were present approximately 3:1 relative to those with the msl10-3G dwarf phenotype (Figure 5C), indicating that the sdm mutations are dominant in the msl10-3G background, at least for this phenotype.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The sdm mutations are dominant in the msl10-3G background, at least for the height phenotype.
claims.source: Furthermore, in the BC1F2 generation, plants with intermediate height (sdm phenotype) were present approximately 3:1 relative to those with the msl10-3G dwarf phenotype (Figure 5C), indicating that the sdm mutations are dominant in the msl10-3G background, at least for this phenotype.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed segregation ratio.

claims.claim: When sdm26 and sdm34 plants were outcrossed to the msl10-1 null allele, plants with the parental msl10-3G phenotype were recovered in the F2 generation.
claims.source: When sdm26 and sdm34 plants were outcrossed to the msl10-1 null allele, plants with the parental msl10-3G phenotype were recovered in the F2 generation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), confirming that the sdm26 and sdm34 lesions are extragenic alleles unlinked to MSL10.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The sdm26 and sdm34 lesions are extragenic alleles unlinked to MSL10.
claims.source: When sdm26 and sdm34 plants were outcrossed to the msl10-1 null allele, plants with the parental msl10-3G phenotype were recovered in the F2 generation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), confirming that the sdm26 and sdm34 lesions are extragenic alleles unlinked to MSL10.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the recovery of the msl10-3G phenotype in the F2 generation.

claims.claim: Ectopic cell death was suppressed in sdm26 and sdm34 leaves compared to those of parental and segregating msl10-3G siblings.
claims.source: Another characteristic phenotype of msl10-3G plants, ectopic cell death, was also suppressed in sdm26 and sdm34 leaves compared to those of parental and segregating msl10-3G siblings, although the sdm mutants exhibited slightly more cell death than WT plants (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: The sdm mutants exhibited slightly more cell death than WT plants.
claims.source: Another characteristic phenotype of msl10-3G plants, ectopic cell death, was also suppressed in sdm26 and sdm34 leaves compared to those of parental and segregating msl10-3G siblings, although the sdm mutants exhibited slightly more cell death than WT plants (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: The whole-genome sequencing strategy consisted of separating BC1F2 plants by phenotype into pools of 50 plants each, extracting genomic DNA from pooled tissue, and sequencing at 80× coverage.
claims.source: The whole-genome sequencing strategy we used to identify the mutations responsible for sdm26 and sdm34 phenotypes consisted of separating BC1F2 plants by phenotype into pools of 50 plants each, extracting genomic DNA from pooled tissue, and sequencing at 80× coverage (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental approach used.

claims.claim: sdm26 and sdm34 are dominant suppressor mutations.
claims.source: As sdm26 and sdm34 are dominant suppressor mutations, we searched for EMS-induced SNPs that (1) had an allele frequency of 0.66 in the pool of plants with the sdm phenotype and (2) were absent in the msl10-3G phenotype pool.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the observed segregation ratios.

claims.claim: Intervals of adjacent SNPs with allele frequencies of 0.66 in the sdm pool and absent in the msl10-3G pool were found on chromosome 1 for sdm26.
claims.source: Intervals of adjacent SNPs with such allele frequencies were found on chromosome 1 for sdm26 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and chromosome 3 for sdm34 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Intervals of adjacent SNPs with allele frequencies of 0.66 in the sdm pool and absent in the msl10-3G pool were found on chromosome 3 for sdm34.
claims.source: Intervals of adjacent SNPs with such allele frequencies were found on chromosome 1 for sdm26 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and chromosome 3 for sdm34 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Clear intervals of linked SNPs with the expected allele frequencies were not identified for the other three presumed extragenic mutants.
claims.source: We failed to identify clear intervals of linked SNPs with the expected allele frequencies for the other three presumed extragenic mutants.
claims.evidence: The manuscript describes the results of the mapping-by-sequencing strategy.

claims.claim: The interval in sdm26 contained 8 genes.
claims.source: The intervals in sdm26 and sdm34 contained 8 and 13 genes, respectively.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the analysis of the genomic intervals identified by mapping-by-sequencing.

claims.claim: The interval in sdm34 contained 13 genes.
claims.source: The intervals in sdm26 and sdm34 contained 8 and 13 genes, respectively.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the analysis of the genomic intervals identified by mapping-by-sequencing.

claims.claim: The sdm26 genome encoded a missense mutation (Ser66→Phe) in the synaptotagmin 5 (SYT5) gene.
claims.source: The sdm26 genome encoded a missense mutation (Ser66→Phe) in the synaptotagmin 5 (SYT5) gene and the sdm34 genome encoded a Gly427→Arg substitution in synaptotagmin 7 (SYT7, CBL1, NTMC2T4; Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The sdm34 genome encoded a Gly427→Arg substitution in synaptotagmin 7 (SYT7, CBL1, NTMC2T4).
claims.source: The sdm26 genome encoded a missense mutation (Ser66→Phe) in the synaptotagmin 5 (SYT5) gene and the sdm34 genome encoded a Gly427→Arg substitution in synaptotagmin 7 (SYT7, CBL1, NTMC2T4; Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: SYT5 and SYT7 are known to interact with each other and with SYT1 at EPCSs.
claims.source: SYT5 and SYT7 are known to interact with each other and with SYT1 at EPCSs (Ishikawa et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Ishikawa et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2020).

claims.claim: The SNPs in SYT5 and SYT7 were promising candidates for causing the suppression of the msl10-3G phenotypes in sdm26 and sdm34.
claims.source: Given these results, and that MSL10 interacts with EPCS proteins (Figures 1 and 2), the SNPs in SYT5 and SYT7 were promising candidates for causing the suppression of the msl10-3G phenotypes in sdm26 and sdm34.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the interaction between MSL10 and EPCS proteins and the known function of SYT5 and SYT7.

claims.claim: It remained possible that lesions elsewhere in the sdm26 and sdm34 intervals were responsible for the suppression of msl10-3G phenotypes.
claims.source: However, it remained possible that lesions elsewhere in these intervals were instead responsible.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about alternative explanations.

claims.claim: SYT5 S66F and SYT7 G427R were expressed from transgenes in unmutagenized msl10-3G plants to recreate the sdm phenotypes.
claims.source: We therefore attempted to recreate the sdm phenotypes by expressing SYT5 S66F and SYT7 G427R from transgenes in unmutagenized msl10-3G plants.
claims.evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental approach used.

claims.claim: sdm-like phenotypes were expected to be seen in the T1 generation because the suppressor mutations in sdm26 and sdm34 plants were dominant.
claims.source: We expected to see sdm-like phenotypes in the T1 generation because the suppressor mutations in sdm26 and sdm34 plants were dominant.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the observed dominance of the sdm mutations.

claims.claim: msl10-3G+SYT5g S66F T1 plants were taller than untransformed msl10-3G plants.
claims.source: As anticipated, msl10-3G+SYT5g S66F and msl10-3+SYT7g G427R T1 plants were taller than untransformed msl10-3G plants (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: msl10-3+SYT7g G427R T1 plants were taller than untransformed msl10-3G plants.
claims.source: As anticipated, msl10-3G+SYT5g S66F and msl10-3+SYT7g G427R T1 plants were taller than untransformed msl10-3G plants (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: The amount of ectopic cell death was suppressed in msl10-3G+SYT5g S66F and msl10-3+SYT7g G427R T1 plants compared to msl10-3G leaves.
claims.source: The amount of ectopic cell death was also suppressed compared to msl10-3G leaves.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: WT SYT5g-mRFP or WT SYT7g-mRFP transgenes had no discernible effect on plant height or ectopic cell death in T1 plants in the msl10-3G background.
claims.source: WT SYT5g-mRFP or WT SYT7g-mRFP transgenes had no discernible effect on plant height or ectopic cell death in T1 plants in the msl10-3G background.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: SYT5 S66F and SYT7 G427R mutations caused suppression of msl10-3G phenotypes in the sdm26 and sdm34 mutants, respectively.
claims.source: These results provide strong evidence that SYT5 S66F and SYT7 G427R mutations caused suppression of msl10-3G phenotypes in the sdm26 and sdm34 mutants, respectively.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that expressing SYT5 S66F and SYT7 G427R in msl10-3G plants recreated the sdm phenotypes.

claims.claim: msl10-3G plants were crossed to null syt5 and syt7 alleles to address whether the sdm26 and sdm34 mutations might be dominant negative.
claims.source: To address whether the sdm26 and sdm34 mutations might be dominant negative, we crossed msl10-3G plants to null syt5 and syt7 alleles (Ishikawa et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental approach used.

claims.claim: Double syt5; msl10-3G mutants resembled msl10-3G plants.
claims.source: Double syt5; msl10-3G and syt7; msl10-3G mutants resembled msl10-3G plants (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: Double syt7; msl10-3G mutants resembled msl10-3G plants.
claims.source: Double syt5; msl10-3G and syt7; msl10-3G mutants resembled msl10-3G plants (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: The inability of null syt5 and syt7 alleles to suppress msl10-3G phenotypes indicates that the sdm26 (SYT5 S66F) and sdm34 (SYT7 G427R) alleles do not cause suppression by impairing the function of WT SYT5 or SYT7.

claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that null syt5 and syt7 alleles did not suppress msl10-3G phenotypes.

claims.claim: The null syt1-2 allele had no effect on msl10-3G growth defects or ectopic death.
claims.source: Additionally, the null syt1-2 allele (Ishikawa et al., 2020) had no effect on msl10-3G growth defects or ectopic death (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The SYT5 S66F and SYT7 G427R point mutations occur in different parts of the synaptotagmin proteins and are not located in any of the predicted functional domains.
claims.source: The SYT5 S66F and SYT7 G427R point mutations occur in different parts of the synaptotagmin proteins and are not located in any of the predicted functional domains (Ishikawa et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2020; UniProt Consortium, 2021; Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: S66 is fully conserved in SYT5 homologs from monocots and dicots.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

results.result: Immunoprecipitation-mass spectrometry identified 1904 peptides mapping to 606 protein groups from MSL10-GFP pulldowns, with 239 proteins having at least 8 peptide spectral matches and a number of proteins significantly enriched compared to wild-type controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C9 describe the experimental workflow and quantitative results from the mass spectrometry experiment. The methods are clearly described (C3-C6), and the quantitative results (C7-C9) are reported with appropriate detail and supported by Figure 1A. The experimental design includes proper controls (mock immunoprecipitations from WT).

results.result: Most proteins identified in MSL10-GFP pulldowns were also pulled down with the inactive MSL107D-GFP variant, and no proteins showed significantly altered abundance between MSL10 and MSL107D proteomes, suggesting interactions are independent of MSL10 cell death-inducing activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C13 are supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and 1B, with appropriate statistical thresholds (fold change > 4, p-value < 0.05). The inference that interactions are independent of cell death activity (C12) is reasonable given the data, though it remains an interpretation rather than direct demonstration.

results.result: VAP27-1, VAP27-3, and SYT1 were among the most enriched proteins in MSL10-GFP pulldowns, with peptide coverage exceeding 30% for MSL10 and VAP27s and 11% for SYT1, and these proteins are known components of plant EPCSs.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C21 report specific findings from the mass spectrometry data with quantitative peptide coverage metrics. The identification of these proteins is supported by the data, and their known association with EPCSs (C17) is appropriately cited to prior literature.

results.result: Twenty percent of proteins co-immunoprecipitating with MSL10-GFP were detected in at least one EPCS interactome (SYT1, VST1, VAP27-1/3, RTNLB3/6), with MSL10 sharing 23, 15, and 14 interacting proteins with VST1, SYT1, and RTNLB3/6 respectively, strongly suggesting MSL10 physically associates with EPCS protein complexes.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C31 describe a meta-analysis comparing the MSL10 interactome with published EPCS interactomes. The quantitative overlap data (C22, C27-C29) are supported by Figure 1B. The inference that MSL10 associates with EPCS complexes (C23, C31) is reasonable given the substantial overlap, though the claim acknowledges this is suggestive rather than definitive.

results.result: Using the yeast mating-based split-ubiquitin system (mbSUS), only NubG-VAP27-1 and NubG-VAP27-3 survived on minimal media when mated with MSL10-Cub among 14 tested proteins, while MSL10-Cub interacted with MSL10-NubG but not with KAT1-NubG or untagged NubG controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C40 describe the mbSUS experimental approach and results. The methodology is appropriate for testing direct protein-protein interactions in yeast (C35-C36). The positive control (MSL10 self-interaction, C37) and negative controls (KAT1, untagged NubG, C38-C39) are appropriate. The selective interaction with VAP27-1 and VAP27-3 (C40) is supported by Figure 2A.

results.result: The interaction between MSL10 and VAP27s was maintained with inactive (MSL107D) and overactive (MSL107A, MSL10S640L) MSL10 variants, and did not require the conserved major sperm protein domains of VAP27s, indicating MSL10 interacts with VAP27-1 and VAP27-3 in a non-canonical way independent of MSL10 signaling activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C47 are supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and 1B. The observation that multiple MSL10 variants interact with VAP27s (C41-C43) supports the inference that interaction is independent of signaling state (C44). The lack of requirement for the MSP domain (C45) and absence of known VAP27-binding motifs (C46) support the conclusion of non-canonical interaction (C47).

results.result: FRET-FLIM analysis showed MSL10-GFP fluorescence lifetime decreased from 2.3 ± 0.1 ns to 1.8 ± 0.2 ns (22% decrease) with mRFP-VAP27-1 and to 1.6 ± 0.3 ns (30% decrease) with mRFP-VAP27-3, while co-expression with free mRFP had no effect, providing additional evidence for direct interaction in plant cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C54 describe FRET-FLIM experiments with appropriate controls. The methodology is sound (C48-C49), the quantitative results are reported with error estimates (C50-C52), the negative control is appropriate (C53), and the fluorescence lifetimes are consistent with prior literature (C54). The decreases in fluorescence lifetime support proximity consistent with direct interaction.

results.result: In stable transgenic Arabidopsis lines and transiently transformed tobacco, approximately 33% of MSL10-GFP co-localized with mRFP-VAP27-3 in leaf epidermal cells, with MSL10-GFP localizing to the plasma membrane and mRFP-VAP27s to the ER, indicating a subpopulation of MSL10 interacts with VAP27s to create EPCSs.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C68 describe co-localization studies in both Arabidopsis and tobacco. The quantitative co-localization data (C59-C60) are supported by Figure 3B using appropriate Mander's overlap coefficients. The partial co-localization (C63) is consistent with a subpopulation interaction (C67). The inference that this interaction creates EPCSs (C68) is logical given the PM localization of MSL10 and ER localization of VAP27s.

results.result: MAPPER-GFP puncta were similar in wild-type and msl10-1 plants but expanded in msl10-3G plants, occupying 13.1 ± 3.1% of cellular area in msl10-3G leaf epidermal cells compared to 8.7 ± 2.9% in wild-type.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C75 describe the effect of MSL10 alleles on EPCS morphology using MAPPER-GFP as a marker. The experimental design is appropriate (C71), and the quantitative results (C72-C75) are supported by Figure 4A-C with statistical analysis. The expansion in msl10-3G but not msl10-1 suggests a gain-of-function effect.

results.result: Genetic crosses between MSL10 mutants and lines overexpressing EPCS proteins revealed genetic interactions, with inability to isolate plants carrying UBQ:VAP27-3-GFP in msl10-1 or msl10-3G backgrounds and fewer msl10-1; UBQ:SYT1-GFP plants than expected by Mendelian segregation.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C79 describe genetic interactions revealed through crossing experiments. The segregation data (C78-C79) are supported by Table 1 with chi-squared statistical analysis showing significant deviations from expected ratios. These genetic interactions provide additional evidence for functional relationships between MSL10 and EPCS proteins.

results.result: SYT1-GFP displayed punctate localization that was unchanged in msl10-1 but expanded in msl10-3G leaf epidermal cells, leading to a modest but significant increase in SYT1-GFP area relative to cellular area, resembling the MAPPER-GFP pattern.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C87 describe the effect of MSL10 alleles on SYT1-GFP localization. The results are supported by Figure 4E-G with statistical analysis showing significant differences. The expansion in msl10-3G but not msl10-1 (C84-C85) parallels the MAPPER-GFP results, and the similarity between patterns (C87) is supported by visual comparison of Figure 4A and 4E.

results.result: MAPPER-GFP-marked EPCSs expanded after 16 hr exposure to 100 mM NaCl in wild-type, msl10-1, and msl10-3G seedlings, and decreased 24 hr after hypo-osmotic shock in all genotypes, indicating MSL10 does not influence EPCS expansion during salinity stress or shrinking after hypo-osmotic shock.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C95 describe EPCS responses to osmotic perturbations. The results are supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and 1B. The similar responses across genotypes (C90, C95) support the inference that MSL10 does not influence these particular EPCS rearrangements (C91), though this is a negative result that should be interpreted cautiously.

results.result: A forward genetic screen of EMS-mutagenized msl10-3G plants identified 40 suppressor mutants (sdm), of which 35 had intragenic mutations in MSL10 and 5 were presumed extragenic, with successful mapping of two extragenic suppressors (sdm26 and sdm34).
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C103 describe the forward genetic screen design and initial results. The screen design is appropriate (C98-C99), the sequencing approach is sound (C100), and the quantitative results (C101-C102) are supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1A. The successful mapping of two extragenic suppressors (C103) sets up subsequent analysis.

results.result: sdm26 and sdm34 mutants showed intermediate height between msl10-3G and wild-type, with BC1F2 plants segregating approximately 3:1 for suppressed versus dwarf phenotypes, and recovery of msl10-3G phenotype in F2 crosses to msl10-1, confirming dominant extragenic suppression with reduced but not eliminated ectopic cell death.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C111 describe the phenotypic characterization of sdm mutants. The height phenotypes (C104-C105) are supported by Figure 5B, the segregation ratios (C106) by Figure 5C, and the dominance inference (C107) is appropriate. The outcross results (C108-C109) confirm extragenic suppression. The cell death phenotypes (C110-C111) are supported by Figure 5D.

results.result: Whole-genome sequencing of pooled BC1F2 plants identified intervals on chromosome 1 (sdm26, 8 genes) and chromosome 3 (sdm34, 13 genes) containing missense mutations in SYT5 (Ser66→Phe) and SYT7 (Gly427→Arg) respectively.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C120 describe the mapping-by-sequencing strategy and identification of causal mutations. The methodology is appropriate for dominant mutations (C112-C113), the mapping results are supported by Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2 (C114-C115), and the specific mutations identified (C119-C120) are supported by Figure 6B. The gene counts (C117-C118) provide context for candidate prioritization.

results.result: Expression of SYT5 S66F or SYT7 G427R transgenes in msl10-3G plants recreated the sdm phenotypes with increased height and suppressed cell death in T1 plants, while wild-type SYT5g-mRFP or SYT7g-mRFP had no effect, providing strong evidence these mutations cause suppression.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C130 describe complementation experiments that validate the causal mutations. The experimental design is appropriate (C124-C125), the results are supported by Figure 6D (C126-C128), the negative control is proper (C129), and the inference of causality (C130) is well-supported by the complementation data.

results.result: Double mutants syt5; msl10-3G and syt7; msl10-3G resembled msl10-3G plants, and null syt1-2 had no effect on msl10-3G phenotypes, indicating the sdm26 and sdm34 alleles do not cause suppression by impairing wild-type SYT function.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C135 describe genetic tests for dominant-negative effects. The experimental design is appropriate (C131), the results are supported by Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and 1B (C132-C133, C135), and the inference that suppression is not through loss of function (C134) is logical given that null alleles do not suppress.

results.result: The sdm mutations did not alter SYT5/SYT7 localization, dynamics, or transcript stability in tobacco, nor MSL10-GFP protein levels in Arabidopsis, indicating suppression occurs through a mechanism other than affecting protein expression, stability, or localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C140-C146 describe characterization of the sdm mutations' effects on protein properties. The localization and dynamics data (C140-C141) are supported by Figure 7—figure supplement 1C and Videos 1-4, transcript stability (C142) by Figure 7—figure supplement 1D, and MSL10 levels (C143-C144) by Figure 7—figure supplement 1E and 1F. The inference (C145-C146) appropriately rules out trivial explanations.

results.result: The larger EPCS area in msl10-3G plants (13.7 ± 4.2%) was not suppressed in sdm26 (13.5 ± 3.7%) or sdm34 leaf epidermal cells, indicating differences in ER-PM connectivity as marked by MAPPER-GFP do not drive the phenotypic differences between wild-type, msl10-3G, and sdm plants.
results.evaluation: Claims C151-C154 describe a key negative result testing whether EPCS expansion drives msl10-3G phenotypes. The experimental design is appropriate (C151), the quantitative results are supported by Figure 7A-D (C152-C153), and the inference (C154) is logical. This is an important finding that rules out a simple model and suggests more complex mechanisms.

results.result: MSL10-GFP has the same electrophysiological and cell death signaling properties as untagged MSL10.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2 establish that the GFP-tagged version used throughout the study is functionally equivalent to untagged MSL10. This is supported by citations to previous studies (Maksaev and Haswell, 2012; Basu et al., 2020b) that characterized these properties. This validation is essential for interpreting all subsequent experiments using MSL10-GFP.

results.result: The partial overlap between MSL10 and other EPCS interactomes may be due to incomplete interactomes, large and difficult-to-survey protein complexes, and/or different EPCS complexes in different cell types or conditions.
results.evaluation: Claim C30 offers speculative explanations for the partial overlap observed in the interactome comparisons. While these are reasonable hypotheses, they are not directly tested in the manuscript. The claim appropriately acknowledges uncertainty by using speculative language, but no experimental evidence is provided to distinguish among these possibilities.

results.result: The SYT5 S66F and SYT7 G427R mutations occur outside predicted functional domains but at conserved residues (S66 fully conserved in SYT5 homologs, G427 partially conserved in SYT7 homologs), suggesting they may be important for structure or function.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C139 describe the location and conservation of the sdm mutations. The domain locations (C136) are supported by Figure 6B and citations, the conservation data (C137-C138) are supported by Figure 6C, and the speculation about importance (C139) is appropriately tentative given the conservation data.
